quote: Wie viel Kugeln {+mit Radius 1+} gehen in einen Würfel (Tetraeder Anordnung, wo an eine Kugel 12 Nachbarkugeln anstossen)
english: How many balls of radius 1 fit into a cube (tetrahedral arrangement, where 12 neighbouring balls touch one ball)
topic: The page completes an induction step (from n to n-1) in the proof of the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality, sketches a circuit for switching a current on and off independently from two or more places, and poses sphere-packing and circle-packing questions together with a related polygon minimization problem.

triage.modern_statement: There are two ways to read this. (a) The literal, elementary reading: count how many unit balls fit in a cube of side a when the balls are placed in the face-centred cubic (cubic close-packed) lattice, where each ball touches 12 others. This is a lattice-point counting exercise. (b) The research version: for a cube of given size, find the largest number N of non-overlapping balls of radius 1 that fit inside it. Equivalently, find the largest common radius r_n of n equal non-overlapping balls in a unit cube, and decide whether arrangements cut from the fcc/ccp lattice are optimal. In the limit of a very large cube, this becomes the Kepler conjecture: the fcc packing, density π/√18, is the densest packing of space.
triage.answered_by: Asymptotic (whole-space) part: Thomas C. Hales proved the Kepler conjecture (announced 1998, published 2005 in Annals of Mathematics). Sphere-packing density is part of Hilbert's 18th problem. Finite 'n spheres in a cube' problem: Schaer (1966) proved optimal packings for n ≤ 9 and later for n = 10. Joós proved n = 14 (Geometriae Dedicata, 2009). Larger n have only computer-found best-known packings (Gensane 2004; Tatarevic 2015). In general it remains open.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 18th problem asks for dense packings of spheres (and tetrahedra). Finding the best sphere packing in three dimensions is the Kepler conjecture.
Hales's series of papers proves the Kepler conjecture: the fcc packing is the densest packing of congruent spheres in three dimensions.
In 1966 Schaer reported packings of k congruent spheres in a unit cube for k ≤ 9.
Joós proved the optimal packing of 14 congruent spheres in a cube (Geometriae Dedicata 140, 2009, 49–80).
Gensane (2004) used a billiard algorithm to list the optimal and best-known packings of n equal spheres in a cube.

Tatarevic (2015) studied cases where n is just below the number of spheres in a regular cubic close-packed (ccp) arrangement. The paper says the densest known arrangements are often assumed to come from ccp by leaving out some spheres, and it gives improved packings.

triage.why: Hilbert asks how many unit balls fit in a cube when they are arranged in the fcc lattice with 12 touching neighbours. Read literally, that is just counting, and it is not stated as a research question. The research question behind it is whether that lattice arrangement is the best possible, and it has two parts. In the infinite limit it is the Kepler conjecture, part of Hilbert's own 18th problem (1900), which Hales solved. For a finite cube, the 'n equal spheres in a cube' problem has proofs only for small n (Schaer; Joós for n = 14). Beyond that there are numerical best-known packings, and papers up to at least 2015 show that ccp-derived arrangements are not always optimal. I did not find any source that discusses this particular diary note, so linking it to these later results is my own reading. Confidence is medium because the note can be read either way: as a counting exercise or as an optimality question.
